The Evidence Room

Maintenance & Alimony Judgments

Rulings on interim maintenance and permanent alimony, how the amount is fixed, and when a claim is reduced or refused because of earning capacity, desertion or concealed income.

36 judgments · 14 from the Supreme Court · updated 25 November 2026

Maintenance claims in India arise under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita), Sections 24 and 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, and the Domestic Violence Act. In Rajnesh v. Neha (2020) the Supreme Court laid down guidelines that apply across these laws, including sworn disclosure of income and assets by both sides.

Maintenance is meant to secure a reasonable standard of living, not to punish. The judgments here cover how interim and permanent amounts are fixed, the weight given to a spouse’s qualifications and earning capacity, the effect of concealing income, maintenance for husbands, and the limits on claims against in-laws.

Maintenance Calcutta HC / Supreme Court
Ankit Saraiya v. Pooja Saraiya (C.R.R. 553 of 2026; 2026 INSC 1227)
April & November 2026

The Calcutta High Court held that a wife living in the matrimonial home cannot also claim alternative-accommodation charges, and set amounts already paid against the child’s maintenance. On appeal, the Supreme Court recorded a ₹75 crore settlement, closed 14 cases between the families under Article 142, and kept the father’s visitation under a parenting plan in the Calcutta High Court format.

Maintenance MP High Court
Wife & Minor Son v. Husband (2026 LiveLaw (MP) 454)
November 2026

Upheld the refusal of maintenance to a wife who is a qualified dentist. Having sufficient cause to live separately does not by itself entitle a wife to maintenance if she can support herself. The child’s ₹30,000 a month was kept in place.

Maintenance Allahabad High Court
VKN v. SRT (Division Bench)
November 2026

Child maintenance is a joint parental obligation. The mother’s income counts when setting each parent’s share, and a father’s duty to pay for schooling “cannot be made a tool for oppression”. The father, earning about ₹37,500 against the mother’s ₹60,000, had his share cut from ₹15,000 to ₹12,000 a month.

Maintenance Supreme Court
Reji Baby v. Subi Mary & Ors. (2026 INSC 918)
August 24, 2026

Quashed a wife’s Domestic Violence Act case as an abuse of process. She had given up all money and maintenance claims in a settlement and a court affidavit before their mutual-consent divorce, and cannot revive them later. The adult daughter, who was not a party to the settlement, keeps her own claims.

Maintenance Supreme Court
A v. B (2026 INSC 822)
August 2026

Held that Provident Fund and Employee Stock Purchase Plan deductions ultimately accrue as benefits to the husband and cannot be excluded when computing income for maintenance — unlike tax.

Maintenance Delhi High Court
X v. Y (CRL.REV.P.(MAT.) 122/2024)
August 2026

Cut interim maintenance from ₹30,000 to ₹25,000 a month even though the husband earns over ₹63 lakh a year, weighing the wife’s MBA, her rental and fixed-deposit income, and the fact that the children live with the husband, who bears their expenses.

Maintenance Supreme Court
Himanshu Chordia v. State of Rajasthan & Anr. (2026 INSC 778)
July 2026

Where a husband produces clear, ex-facie evidence of the wife’s adulterous relationship under Section 125(4) CrPC, courts cannot defer that defence until final adjudication — it must be decided even at the interim maintenance stage.

Maintenance Madhya Pradesh High Court
Ranu v. Himanshu — Parents Who Arrange a Child Marriage Share Liability
May 2026

Enhanced a child-marriage victim’s maintenance from ₹2,000 to ₹6,000/month, holding that parents who were instrumental in solemnising the marriage cannot escape liability: ‘If the husband feels hardships then he has to take help of those parents who were instrumental in performing the child marriage.’

Maintenance Rajasthan High Court
Arvind Kumar v. Smt. Namita — Husband Entitled to Wife’s Employment Records
April 6, 2026

Husband is entitled to seek production of wife’s employment and salary records to contest a maintenance claim. Courts cannot determine fair maintenance without full income disclosure by both parties.

Maintenance P&H High Court
Anu Aggarwal v. Sushant Aggarwal — Maintenance Denied for Concealing Income
January 13, 2026

Court dismissed maintenance revision petition — wife was highly qualified and concealed her income and assets. Section 125 CrPC cannot be used as a tool by financially capable spouses who suppress their means.

Maintenance Supreme Court
Rakhi Sadhukhan v. Raja Sadhukhan
May 2025

Inflation-indexed permanent alimony — 5% increase every 2 years. Matrimonial home transferred to wife. Sets standard for long-term alimony calculations.

Maintenance Delhi High Court
Megha Khetrapal v. Rajat Kapoor (CRL.REV.P. 273/2023)
March 19, 2025

Upheld the refusal of interim maintenance to a wife with a master’s degree from Australia and past work at KPMG Dubai, who left her qualifications and earlier jewellery business out of her income affidavit. A well-educated wife ought not to remain idle solely to gain maintenance.

Maintenance Supreme Court
SC — Maintenance in Void Marriages
Feb 2025

Permanent alimony and interim maintenance can be awarded even in marriages declared void under Section 11 HMA. Section 25 applies to all decrees regardless of marriage validity.

Shakti v. Anita (2025) 3 SCC 728
2025

Maintenance Supreme Court
Parvin Kumar Jain v. Anju Jain
Dec 2024

Consolidated 8 factors for calculating permanent alimony — status of parties, earning capacity, assets, needs and more — building on Rajnesh v. Neha (2020) to bring uniformity to spousal support. ‘Not a straitjacket formula.’

Maintenance Supreme Court
Kiran Jyot Maini v. Anish Pramod Patel (2024 INSC 530)
July 2024

Permanent alimony “should not be penal”; its purpose is to secure a decent standard of living. The Court fixed a one-time ₹2 crore, well below the wife’s ₹5–7 crore demand, after weighing both spouses’ incomes, assets and liabilities.

Kalyan Sah v. Mosmat Rashmi Priya — Daughter-in-Law Cannot Claim from Father-in-Law
January 19, 2023

A daughter-in-law cannot claim maintenance directly from her father-in-law under Section 125 CrPC — the liability lies with the husband, not his parents.

Bhagyashri v. Jagdish Jaiswal & Anr.
February 26, 2022

Shivanand Gurannavar v. Basavva
February 17, 2022

Maintenance Supreme Court
Rajnesh v. Neha (2021) 2 SCC 324
Nov 2020

Comprehensive guidelines to govern maintenance across all matrimonial statutes. Where maintenance is claimed under multiple laws simultaneously, courts must account for and set off amounts already paid so a husband does not pay twice. A standardised Affidavit of Disclosure of Assets and Liabilities made mandatory for both parties.

Sejalben Tejasbhai Chovatiya v. State of Gujarat — Perjury for Concealing Income

Wife claimed to be an unemployed housewife with no income while seeking maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, despite evidence of business income and fixed deposits. High Court refused to quash the perjury complaint, holding that prosecution under Sections 191/193 IPC was warranted for concealing income from the court.

Rani Sethi v. Sunil Sethi
2011

Upheld interim maintenance to a husband under Section 24 HMA (₹20,000/month plus a car) where the wife had greater means — a high-profile application of the Act’s gender-neutral maintenance provision.

Maintenance Delhi High Court
Sanjay Bhardwaj & Ors. v. State & Anr.
August 27, 2010

Set aside interim maintenance against a husband who had lost his job abroad. Where both spouses are equally qualified (both held MBAs), an unemployed husband cannot be treated differently from an unemployed wife, and a court cannot tell him to ‘beg, borrow or steal’ to pay. There is no presumption that every failed marriage involves dowry or violence.

August 26, 2003

Set aside maintenance for a wife who left the matrimonial home without sufficient reason. Her dowry and cruelty allegations had no support in the evidence, and courts must decide on the record, not on conjecture. The son’s maintenance continued.

Using these judgments

Official Court Copy opens the judgment PDF from the Supreme Court’s own website. Full Judgment opens the complete judgment text (Indian Kanoon, or a PDF copy of the order). Read Report opens a news or legal-blog summary where no full text is linked yet.

To rely on a judgment in court, cite it by its case number or citation; the court’s registry can issue a certified copy. Check that it has not been overturned or modified on appeal. The one-line summaries on this page are for information only and are not legal advice.
